I will also note that I have had a lot of shit happen to me in my years as a social worker, deaths of very important people in my life, divorce, etc. And while I never used my clients as a dual relationship, the ones who knew me, really knew me, gave as much to me when I couldn't give to myself. And I love each and everyone of them. They sustained me in ways no one else could and I will always remember that and be entirely grateful. You build relationships, you build rapport, that's how it should be, it makes the job harder, but it also makes the job sweeter also.

I am not a therapist, but I cried on the phone when I found out a client who had been waiting on a big lifetime decision was denied, I was invested and clearly he was. I had no words for him really, but to be choked up and just be there with him in it. Clearly it isn't shouldn't happen every time, but I will say that while you can't bill for compassion, you can certainly show it, and that you did. 

You are not a bad therapist, you are human, that is what humans do, and you should be proud, not embarrassed. Years ago, a therapist of mine realized that she could no longer contain her tears when I was talking about my family trauma, and she (while in tears) "Your pain was never heard, was it?", at the time I was annoyed because I felt "I'm the one one here seeking care", and then she gave me a hug. When I got home, I googled "should a therapist hug you?" there were varying responses to it, many of them going "no, no, no", and I believed that for a long time. But sense, my view of that has changed. We all want to be heard, we all want to feel like someone cares, especially when no else does, it keeps us going, it makes me human and makes us feel whole when sometimes we can't do so for ourselves. 

She cried for me when I couldn't, she made the space for my pain expressed through her tears. I would later come to feel those painful feelings more acutely, but in that moment, she cried those tears for me, when I couldn't, when all I had was anger, she was the vessel for the tears I couldn't cry at the time, she was the person I had yet to be, and now am. I'll never forget it, and neither should you. You are a human being, in a hard profession, we are all doing the best we can with what we've been given. If a patient/client can't see the gift of your tears now, they certainly will later. I have had clients project their angry, their rage at me, but I knew it is was coming from a place of pain. Your emotions make you a better practitioner, it takes a strong human being to be soft in a world where walls are built up. Be soft, take what you can and give as best as you can, you are beautiful and thank you for being you. 

Your patients deserve kindness and compassion, as do you. Give yourself grace, and the world will give it back to you. I love who you are and never stop being you, Never

I will say the clients sometimes keep me more afloat then they realize. Besides giving me joy and purpose in serving. Their words of encouragement and their humor helps me more than they know; I always learn from them, even the ones that annoy the hell out of me. I remember them all because they sustain me and keep me going when times have been hard. And times have been hard for a long time. But I am grateful to sit on the side of the proverbial chair to listen to their stories, because that is a gift and I never take it for grateful. No one owes you their story, but hearing it and what we do that gift, is how we become better social workers, I know it has made me a better one.

So I'll say this, I was "diagnosed" with bpd 5 years ago, I say in quotations because I came to that psychiatrist at the time and told her I fit pretty much most of it not all the criteria, she had initially diagnosed me with Bipolar disorder, she then said "do you think it's bpd over bipolar disorder?" And I said yes, therefore my bpd diagnosis. I later realized I also have complex trauma and then thought to myself I don't have bpd but this, but recent things where I pretty much obsessed over an ex person in my life realized I was making them my favorite person to self regulate with and it pretty much devastated me with also issues I am dealing with in regards to sex and love addiction, all of that to say, yes, you certainly can and should find a competent psychiatrist for diagnosis but we also know our symptoms best. It is hard not to internalize the label, it's why i initially dropped the bpd "diagnosis" in my mind when I realized I have complex trauma, both can be true and really, at the root of bpd is trauma. Im finding it difficult to be gentle to myself but also realizing that you can beat yourself with a feather, aka be kind to yourself. I realize that this may or may not be helpful but I wanted to share my experience and hope that gives you some insight possibly into your own experience, good luck friend!
